doc.title: Alan Broadbent interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 26, 2023

title: 'Variations on a Scene' and Mahler's effect on him
summary: He recalls writing 'Variations on a Scene' for the Houston Symphony at 23, and says it predates his discovery of Mahler.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Back in 1974 I think you did a piece called “Variations on a Scene” —
Which involved, it was a chamber group and the Woody Herman Orchestra and that was a lot to bite off at that time, wasn’t it?

No, that was the Houston Symphony Orchestra. That was a huge thing. Yeah, well I wouldn’t do that anymore. But listen, again, there’s some very — when I listen to it again — I was 23 — there’s some quite beautiful moments [plays]. There’s a big theme that comes out in the middle, yeah okay kid. The rest, the big ending —
I’m impressed that you can pull that out of your memory like that.

I was too, I’m going uh oh, wait a minute. I do remember, Monk. And with all of this my ending and everything was pre-B.M. which was a cataclysmic cathartic event in my life. All of that “Variations on a Scene” and the ending of it all was before-Mahler. And you know so —
Are you saying that your ears were introduced to Mahler and that had an effect on you?

Well he had a profound effect on me from the word go. And it makes my attempts seem so pretentious. But you know I have to think of it as just a kid who’s having fun writing and doesn’t know any better. Now I know better.
